Department of Endoscopy, Fukushima Medical University Hospital Fukushima Japan ([ROR:012eh0r35](https://ror.org/012eh0r35)) † Corresponding author ## Abstract Background:Post-endoscopic retrograde cholangiopancreatography (ERCP) pancreatitis (PEP) is a severe and deadly adverse event following ERCP. The ideal method for predicting PEP risk before ERCP has yet to be identified. We aimed to establish a simple PEP risk score model (SuPER model: Support for PEP Reduction) that can be applied before ERCP.Methods:This multicenter study enrolled 2074 patients who underwent ERCP. Among them, 1037 patients each were randomly assigned to the development and validation cohorts. In the development cohort, the risk score model for predicting PEP was established via logistic regression analysis. In the validation cohort, the performance of the model was assessed.Results:In the development cohort, five PEP risk factors that could be identified before ERCP were extracted and assigned weights according to their respective regression coefficients: –2 points for pancreatic calcification, 1 point for female sex, and 2 points for intraductal papillary mucinous neoplasm, a native papilla of Vater, or the pancreatic duct procedures (treated as ‘planned pancreatic duct procedures’ for calculating the score before ERCP). The PEP occurrence rate was 0% among low-risk patients (≤0 points), 5.5% among moderate-risk patients (1–3 points), and 20.2% among high-risk patients (4–7 points). In the validation cohort, the C statistic of the risk score model was 0.71 (95% CI 0.64–0.78), which was considered acceptable. The PEP risk classification (low, moderate, and high) was a significant predictive factor for PEP that was independent of intraprocedural PEP risk factors (precut sphincterotomy and inadvertent pancreatic duct cannulation) (OR 4.2, 95% CI 2.8–6.3; p<0.01).Conclusions:The PEP risk score allows an estimation of the risk of PEP prior to ERCP, regardless of whether the patient has undergone pancreatic duct procedures. This simple risk model, consisting of only five items, may aid in predicting and explaining the risk of PEP before ERCP and in preventing PEP by allowing selection of the appropriate expert endoscopist and useful PEP prophylaxes.Funding:No external funding was received for this work. ## Introduction Endoscopic retrograde cholangiopancreatography (ERCP) is widely performed as an important diagnostic and therapeutic procedure for pancreaticobiliary diseases. Among endoscopic procedures, ERCP-related procedures are relatively risky. The high-risk adverse events of ERCP include duodenal perforation and bleeding after endoscopic sphincterotomy (EST) and post-ERCP pancreatitis (PEP). The rate of PEP occurrence is 3.1–13.0% (Andriulli et al., 2007; Freeman et al., 1996; Glomsaker et al., 2013; Katsinelos et al., 2014; Kochar et al., 2015; Loperfido et al., 1998). PEP can even become life-threatening. The fatality rate of PEP is 0.1–0.7% (Andriulli et al., 2007; Kochar et al., 2015). Therefore, the decision to perform ERCP should be made carefully, considering each patient’s risk factors for PEP. To predict an individual patient’s PEP risk, six scoring systems have been devised (Archibugi et al., 2023; Chiba et al., 2021; DiMagno et al., 2013; Friedland et al., 2002; Fujita et al., 2021; Zheng et al., 2020). The first risk scoring system for PEP occurrence was established in 2002. In that study, pain during the procedure, pancreatic duct cannulation, a history of PEP, and the number of cannulation attempts were identified as risk factors for PEP. After the first scoring system was reported, each new scoring system used risk factors that were extracted via multivariate analyses. These included various patient characteristics before ERCP and postprocedural risk factors. Postprocedural risk factors, such as precut sphincterotomy, procedure time, and difficult cannulation, have been proposed, but it is difficult to predict these risk factors and determine the PEP risk before ERCP. Thus, a new prediction scoring system for PEP before ERCP is desirable. If the risk of PEP can be predicted before ERCP, then the expert endoscopist can perform ERCP from the start, and high-PEP-risk procedures (e.g., precut sphincterotomy, multiple cannulation attempts, and inadvertent pancreatic duct cannulation) can be avoided (Testoni et al., 2010; Wang et al., 2009). If biliary cannulation without the use of at least one high-PEP-risk procedure is difficult, other treatments (e.g., percutaneous transhepatic biliary drainage [PTBD] or endoscopic ultrasound [EUS]-guided biliary drainage [EUS-BD]) could be considered. Therefore, we aimed to establish a PEP prediction model using only risk factors that can be gathered before ERCP. Our model was developed and validated with multicenter data from Japan. ## Methods We performed a multicenter retrospective study at six institutions in Japan. This study was approved by the institutional review board of Fukushima Medical University and that of each partner medical institution (number 2453). The analysis used anonymous clinical data obtained after all the participants agreed to treatment with written consent; thus, patients were not required to provide informed consent for the study. The details of the study can be found on the homepage of Fukushima Medical University. ### Patients Among 2176 patients who underwent ERCP between November 2020 and October 2022, 2074 were included in this study. The other 102 patients were excluded for the following reasons: history of choledochojejunostomy, acute pancreatitis, choledochoduodenal fistula, difficulty finding the Vater papilla, history of pancreatojejunostomy, or history of pancreatogastrostomy (Figure 1). The predictive PEP score is not necessary for the excluded patients. The reasons were as follows. Biliary duct cannulation was not attempted in patients for whom it was difficult to identify the Vater papilla. The biliary tract was separated from the pancreas in patients with a history of choledochojejunostomy, pancreatojejunostomy, or pancreatogastrostomy. PEP risk was thought to be clearly low in these patients and patients who underwent bile duct cannulation via the choledochoduodenal fistula. PEP diagnosis is difficult in patients with acute pancreatitis, whose diagnosis is currently in progress. ![Figure 1.](https://cdn.elifesciences.org/articles/101604/elife-101604-fig1-v1.jpg) **Figure 1.:** ERCP, endoscopic retrograde cholangiopancreatography. ### Study design We randomly sampled 50% of the patients as the development cohort and 50% as the validation cohort (Figure 1). In the development cohort, we established a risk scoring system for predicting PEP before ERCP, which was named the support for PEP reduction model (SuPER model). The validation cohort was used to confirm the effectiveness of the scoring system. PEP diagnosis and severity were assessed according to Cotton’s criteria (Cotton et al., 1991). Patients who experienced abdominal pain and had hyperamylasemia (more than three times the normal upper limit) at least 24 hr after ERCP were diagnosed with PEP. Mild PEP was defined as pancreatitis that required prolongation of the planned hospitalization by 2–3 days. Moderate PEP was defined as pancreatitis that required 4–10 days of hospitalization. Severe PEP was defined as pancreatitis that required more than 10 days of hospitalization or intervention or hemorrhagic pancreatitis, phlegmon, or pseudocysts. To establish the risk score, the risk factors for PEP were investigated via data from the development cohort. To determine the PEP risk score, factors that might be associated with PEP occurrence were investigated. To predict the PEP risk score before ERCP, factors related to patient characteristics and previously scheduled procedures, as reported in the Japanese guidelines for acute pancreatitis and PEP, were selected (Itoi et al., 2024; Takada et al., 2022). The patients’ risk factors included age <50 years, female sex, a history of pancreatitis, a history of PEP, a history of gastrectomy, pancreatic cancer, intraductal papillary mucinous neoplasm (IPMN), a native papilla of Vater, absence of chronic pancreatitis (CP), normal serum bilirubin (≤1.2 mg/dl), and periampullary diverticulum (Ding et al., 2015; Freeman et al., 2001; Freeman et al., 1996; Fujita et al., 2022; Fujita et al., 2021; Masci et al., 2003; Wang et al., 2009; Williams et al., 2007; Zheng et al., 2020). Pancreatic divisum was excluded from the patient risk factor list because pancreatic divisum was observed in only two patients. Pancreatic calcification and a diameter of the main pancreatic duct >3 mm were considered to indicate CP (Beyer et al., 2023; Sarner and Cotton, 1984). These imaging findings were confirmed by CT, MRI, and EUS before ERCP. The CT and MRI findings were reviewed by radiologists. IPMNs were diagnosed according to the results of CT, MRI, and EUS. As pre-ERCP prophylaxes for PEP, protease inhibitors (gabexate mesilate or nafamostat mesilate), intravenous hydration, and NSAID suppositories have been used (Fujita et al., 2022). As planned procedure-related risk factors, EST, endoscopic papillary balloon dilation (EPBD), endoscopic papillary large balloon dilation (EPLBD) using a ≥12 mm balloon catheter (Itoi et al., 2018), biliary stone removal, ampullectomy, biliary stent material (plastic stent, self-expandable metallic stent [SEMS], or covered SEMS [CSEMS]), inside stent placement, and procedures on the pancreatic duct were evaluated (Freeman et al., 2001; Freeman et al., 1996; Harewood et al., 2005; Kato et al., 2022; Masci et al., 2003; Masci et al., 2001; Testoni et al., 2010; Williams et al., 2007). A biliary stent above the Vater papilla was also assessed as a prophylactic measure against PEP (Ishiwatari et al., 2013). To demonstrate the independence of the established risk classification, the relationships between it and intraprocedural PEP risk factors (including precut sphincterotomy and inadvertent pancreatic duct cannulation) (Testoni et al., 2010; Wang et al., 2009) were investigated. Because of the retrospective nature of the data, the exact number of cannulations and the number of cannulation attempts were not available. Therefore, multiple cannulation attempts and a prolonged cannulation time could not be investigated as intraprocedural PEP risk factors. ### Sample size The primary aim of this study was to establish a PEP prediction model that could be used to calculate a risk score before ERCP. To construct a prediction model via logistic regression analysis, 10 events per explanatory variable were needed (Wynants et al., 2015). Seven variables were evaluated in the development cohort, so 70 PEP patients were included. Five variables were evaluated in the validation cohort, so 50 PEP patients were necessary. According to a previous systematic review, the rate of PEP occurrence was 9.7% (Kochar et al., 2015). Therefore, at least 722 and 521 patients were included in the development and validation cohorts, respectively. ### Statistical analysis In the development cohort, univariate and multivariate logistic regression analyses were performed to identify the risk factors for PEP. The factors that had a p-value<0.10 in the univariate analysis were included in the multivariate analysis. To construct the scoring system for PEP risk, the factors with p<0.10 in the multivariate analysis were ultimately included in the risk score model. The factors selected in the multivariate analysis were assigned points according to the regression coefficient (each variable’s risk points = the ratio of the variable’s regression coefficient/minimum regression coefficient). The sum of the assigned points was calculated for each patient, and the patients were classified into three groups (low risk, moderate risk, and high risk) according to the expected rate of PEP occurrence (Friedland et al., 2002). The risk classification system (SuPER model) was also applied to the validation cohort. With respect to both the development and validation cohorts, the effectiveness of the risk score model was evaluated as follows. The correlations between the risk score, risk classification, and PEP occurrence were evaluated via the Cochran–Armitage trend test. The predictive accuracy of the risk score was assessed via the C statistic. The goodness of fit of the model was evaluated via the Hosmer‒Lemeshow test. The independence of the established risk classification from the unexpected intraprocedural PEP risk factors was assessed via multivariate logistic regression analyses. Patients with missing data for variables selected in the risk score model were removed from the final cohort. Statistical analyses were performed using EZR version 1.62 (Saitama Medical Centre, Jichi Medical University, Saitama, Japan) and SPSS version 26.0 (IBM Corp., Armonk, NY). A p-value<0.05 indicats statistical significance. ## Results ### Patient characteristics and ERCP outcomes in each cohort The patient characteristics and ERCP outcomes of each cohort are shown in Table 1. A total of 1037 patients were assigned to each of the development and validation cohorts, including 70 (6.8%) and 64 (6.2%) patients diagnosed with PEP, respectively. Age, history of pancreatitis, and procedures involving the pancreatic duct were significantly different between the development cohort and the validation cohort. ### Validation of the PEP risk scoring system The risk score was associated with PEP occurrence in the validation cohort (p<0.01, Cochran–Armitage trend test) (Table 3). We found that 2.4% (8/331) of the patients at low risk, 5.3% (27/513) of those at moderate risk, and 18.0% (29/161) of those at high risk experienced PEP. The risk classification was also correlated with PEP occurrence in the validation cohort (p<0.01, Cochran–Armitage trend test). The C statistic of the risk score was 0.71, which was also high in the validation cohort (Table 4). The PEP risk score model showed good fitness according to the Hosmer–Lemeshow test (p=0.40). According to the above results, the preprocedural PEP risk can be calculated, as shown in Figure 2. The pancreatic duct procedure was treated as a ‘planned pancreatic duct procedure’. Otherwise, we can calculate both the PEP risk score, which involves the pancreatic duct procedure, and the score, which does not involve the pancreatic duct procedure. ![Figure 2.](https://cdn.elifesciences.org/articles/101604/elife-101604-fig2-v1.jpg) **Figure 2.:** ERCP, endoscopic retrograde cholangiopancreatography; IPMN, intraductal papillary mucinous neoplasm; PEP, post-ERCP pancreatitis. ### Risk classification and unexpected PEP risk factors The relationships between the established risk classification and intraprocedural PEP risk factors are shown in Supplementary file 1. For all patients in the development cohort and the validation cohort, the risk classification was significantly associated with the occurrence of PEP. On the other hand, precut sphincterotomy and inadvertent pancreatic duct cannulation were not significantly associated with the occurrence of PEP. ## Discussion In this multicenter study, we aimed to establish a preprocedural PEP prediction model. As a result, we created a risk scoring system (the SuPER model) using five items that could be measured before performing ERCP. The term ‘pancreatic duct procedures’ was ‘planned pancreatic duct procedures’ in the model. When unintended pancreatic duct procedures are considered, we can calculate both the PEP risk score with pancreatic duct procedures and that without pancreatic duct procedures. With this score, PEP occurrence can be accurately predicted to some degree. Although the development cohort and validation cohort had significantly different patient characteristics and ERCP outcomes, the risk score was good in both cohorts. In addition, the established PEP risk classification was associated with PEP occurrence independent of unpredictable intraprocedural PEP risk procedures. This risk scoring and classification of PEP have several advantages. First, the score is calculated using only five items, all of which can be easily assessed via medical interviews and imaging (e.g., CT). One scoring system included sphincter of Oddi dysfunction (SOD) as a test item (DiMagno et al., 2013). The diagnosis of SOD requires sphincter of Oddi manometry and fulfillment of the criteria for biliary pain, but sphincter of Oddi manometry is not widely used (Cotton et al., 2016). The diagnostic criterion for biliary pain included 8 items, and that for SOD included 15 items. Among the items of the SuPER risk scoring system, pancreatic calcification was assigned –2 points. Its low weighting could be explained by the following. The international conceptual model of CP can be divided into four stages: acute pancreatitis–recurrent acute pancreatitis, early CP, established CP, and end-stage CP (Whitcomb et al., 2016). Established CP patients have already passed the acute pancreatitis–recurrent acute pancreatitis course, and pancreatic calcification has been reported in established CP patients. Acinar dysfunction has also been observed in these patients (Whitcomb et al., 2016). Therefore, patients with pancreatic calcification may have a lower incidence of PEP. Second, the SuPER risk score can be determined before the ERCP procedure, as the established risk classification was found to be the sole significant factor predicting the occurrence of PEP independent of intraprocedural PEP risk factors. As described in the Background section, precut sphincterotomy, multiple cannulation attempts, and a cannulation time greater than 10 min were identified as high-risk factors that cannot be accounted for prior to ERCP (Testoni et al., 2010; Wang et al., 2009). Although the established PEP risk classification was independent of the included intraprocedural risk factors (precut sphincterotomy and inadvertent pancreatic duct cannulation), detailed data on the number of cannulation attempts and the cannulation time were not available. Therefore, to avoid intraoperative procedures associated with a high risk of PEP occurrence, an expert endoscopist can initially perform ERCP for high-PEP-risk patients. In addition, PEP prophylaxis can be administered beforehand for high-PEP-risk patients. As effective prophylaxes for PEP, rectal non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drug (NSAID) and pancreatic stent placement have been reported (Akshintala et al., 2021; Choi et al., 2023; Elmunzer et al., 2008; Koshitani et al., 2022; Murray et al., 2003; Sperna Weiland et al., 2022; Sugimoto et al., 2019; Yang et al., 2020). In this report, rectal NSAID use was not identified as a significant factor preventing PEP. One reason for this is that in past reports describing the use of rectal NSAIDs to prevent PEP, patients at high risk for PEP were often treated. In contrast, this study included all patients who underwent ERCP. Another reason might be the difference in dose. 100 mg of rectal diclofenac have been used in most past reports, whereas the efficacy of low-dose rectal diclofenac (25–50 mg) for preventing PEP is under discussion (Maeda et al., 2021; Okuno et al., 2018; Otsuka et al., 2012; Sakai et al., 2023; Takaori et al., 2021; Tomoda et al., 2021). In this study, 12.5–50 mg of diclofenac was used. In Japan, the approved diclofenac dose covered by insurance is 50 mg or less, with the dose typically being lower for elderly patients. Therefore, diclofenac doses ranging from 12.5 to 50 mg were prescribed by the doctors depending on the age and size of the patients. Pancreatic stent placement itself is one of the procedures performed on the pancreatic duct and is a higher-risk procedure for PEP than endoscopic biliary procedures without an approach to the pancreatic duct (Supplementary file 2). Moreover, pancreatic stent placement has become a prophylactic treatment for PEP in patients who have undergone pancreatography or wire placement to the pancreatic duct (Mazaki et al., 2014; Sugimoto et al., 2019). As described above, pancreatic stent placement was performed along with high-risk-PEP procedures (i.e., guidewire placement to the pancreatic duct or pancreatography); therefore, pancreatic stent placement was grouped with the other endoscopic retrograde pancreatography procedures as ‘procedures on the pancreatic duct’. In a recent randomized trial involving 1950 patients, the combination of rectal NSAIDs and prophylactic pancreatic stents was more effective for preventing PEP than NSAIDs alone (Elmunzer et al., 2024). For high-PEP-risk patients with high scores, the combination of prophylactic methods might be desirable. This study has several limitations. First, the study was retrospective, and there were missing data. However, the results reported are trustworthy. The percentage of patients who did not meet the inclusion criteria was not greater than 5%, and the percentage of missing data was not greater than 1%. As described in the ‘Methods’ section, patients with missing data for the variables selected in the risk score model were removed from the final cohort. The reliability of the SuPER risk score model was also statistically confirmed. Second, some factors cannot be assessed before ERCP. Additional procedures can be conducted during ERCP, and unplanned pancreatography is often performed in patients who are scheduled for endoscopic cholangiography or biliary treatment. However, the established PEP risk classification was independent of the included intraprocedural risk factors. A planned procedure for accessing the pancreatic duct is listed in the SuPER risk model. Therefore, we can predict the SuPER risk score and classification of patients regardless of whether they have undergone pancreatic duct procedures. Third, this study was performed in a single country. In the future, prospective validation studies over wider geographical regions are needed. In conclusion, a simple and useful PEP scoring system (SuPER model) with only five clinical items was developed in this multicenter study. This scoring system may aid in predicting and explaining PEP risk and in selecting appropriate prophylaxes for PEP and endoscopic pancreatobiliary procedures for each patient.

Strengths:

results.result: A multicenter retrospective study was conducted at six institutions in Japan, enrolling 2074 patients who underwent ERCP between November 2020 and October 2022. These patients were randomly split into development (n=1037) and validation (n=1037) cohorts after excluding 102 patients based on specific criteria.
results.evaluation: Claims C7, C8, C21, C23-C25, and C155 provide consistent information about study design, enrollment, and patient allocation. The study design is clearly described with appropriate exclusion criteria and random allocation to cohorts, supported by Figure 1.

results.result: Five pre-procedural risk factors for PEP were identified through multivariate logistic regression analysis in the development cohort: female sex (1 point), IPMN (2 points), native papilla of Vater (2 points), pancreatic calcification (-2 points), and procedures on the pancreatic duct (2 points). These factors were selected based on p<0.10 in multivariate analysis and assigned points proportional to their regression coefficients.
results.evaluation: Claims C9-C14 and C37-C46 provide detailed statistical results from univariate and multivariate analyses. The methodology (C122-C124) is clearly described, and the factor selection and point assignment are appropriately justified by the regression coefficients shown in Table 2.

results.result: In the development cohort, the SuPER model stratified patients into three risk groups with PEP rates of 0% (low risk, ≤0 points, 0/327 patients), 5.5% (moderate risk, 1-3 points, 27/492 patients), and 20.2% (high risk, 4-7 points, 39/193 patients). The model showed good discrimination (C-statistic 0.77, 95% CI 0.72-0.82) and calibration (Hosmer-Lemeshow test p=0.59).
results.evaluation: Claims C15-C17 and C83-C85 provide consistent PEP rates across risk groups. The statistical validation (C47-C49) demonstrates significant correlation with PEP occurrence and good model performance. Data are consistent between text and Table 3.

results.result: In the validation cohort, the SuPER model demonstrated acceptable performance with a C-statistic of 0.71 (95% CI 0.64-0.78) and good calibration (Hosmer-Lemeshow test p=0.40). PEP rates were 2.4% (8/331) for low-risk, 5.3% (27/513) for moderate-risk, and 18.0% (29/161) for high-risk patients, with significant correlation between risk classification and PEP occurrence (p<0.01).
results.evaluation: Claims C18-C19 and C50-C54 demonstrate successful validation of the model in an independent cohort. The C-statistic of 0.71 is appropriately characterized as acceptable, and the risk stratification maintained statistical significance. The slightly higher PEP rate in the validation low-risk group (2.4% vs 0%) is acknowledged but does not invalidate the model.

results.result: The SuPER risk classification was independently associated with PEP occurrence (OR 4.2, 95% CI 2.8-6.3; p<0.01) after adjusting for intraprocedural risk factors (precut sphincterotomy and inadvertent pancreatic duct cannulation), which themselves were not significantly associated with PEP in this study.
results.evaluation: While claims C20, C66, and C99-C101 report that the risk classification was independent of intraprocedural factors, the finding that precut sphincterotomy and inadvertent pancreatic duct cannulation were not significant contradicts established literature (C55-C56). This may reflect study limitations (C118-C119) regarding incomplete data on cannulation attempts, or could indicate confounding by the prophylactic measures used.

results.result: PEP occurred in 6.8% (70/1037) of the development cohort and 6.2% (64/1037) of the validation cohort. Most cases were mild (60 and 53 cases respectively), with fewer moderate (8 and 7 cases) and severe (2 and 4 cases) cases. The cohorts differed significantly in age, history of pancreatitis, and pancreatic duct procedures.
results.evaluation: Claims C34-C36 and C132-C134, C136 provide consistent baseline data from Table 1. The PEP rates are within the expected range based on prior literature (C2, C33), and the severity distribution is clearly documented. The differences between cohorts (C36) are acknowledged but did not prevent successful validation.

results.result: PEP was diagnosed using Cotton's criteria, requiring abdominal pain and hyperamylasemia (>3× upper limit of normal) at least 24 hours after ERCP. Severity was classified as mild (2-3 days additional hospitalization), moderate (4-10 days), or severe (>10 days or complications).
results.evaluation: Claims C26-C30 describe standard, well-established diagnostic criteria for PEP with appropriate citation (Cotton et al., 1991). The definitions are clear and consistent with accepted clinical practice.

results.result: Chronic pancreatitis was defined by pancreatic calcification or main pancreatic duct diameter >3 mm on imaging (CT, MRI, EUS). IPMN was diagnosed using the same imaging modalities, with findings reviewed by radiologists.
results.evaluation: Claims C31 and C113-C115 describe appropriate diagnostic criteria for CP and IPMN with supporting citations (C31). The use of multiple imaging modalities and radiologist review (C114) enhances diagnostic accuracy.

results.result: Sample size was calculated based on the requirement of 10 events per variable for logistic regression. With 7 variables in development and 5 in validation, and an expected PEP rate of 9.7%, at least 722 and 521 patients were needed in each cohort respectively.
results.evaluation: Claims C32-C33 and C120-C121 describe appropriate sample size calculation methodology with supporting citations. The actual enrollment (1037 per cohort) exceeded the minimum requirements, providing adequate statistical power.

results.result: The protective effect of pancreatic calcification (assigned -2 points) is explained by the chronic pancreatitis disease model, where established CP patients with calcification have passed the acute/recurrent pancreatitis stage and exhibit acinar dysfunction, potentially reducing PEP susceptibility.
results.evaluation: Claims C60-C63 and C144 provide a biologically plausible explanation for the negative association between pancreatic calcification and PEP, supported by citation to the international CP conceptual model (Whitcomb et al., 2016). The inference (C63) is reasonable given the data (C43-C44) and cited framework.

results.result: Rectal NSAID use was not identified as a significant protective factor in this study. The authors attribute this to: (1) inclusion of all ERCP patients rather than only high-risk patients as in prior studies, and (2) use of lower diclofenac doses (12.5-50 mg) compared to the 100 mg used in most prior reports, with dosing based on patient age and size due to Japanese insurance regulations.
results.evaluation: Claims C93-C98 and C145-C146 provide a reasonable explanation for the negative finding regarding NSAIDs. The dose difference is well-documented (C94-C98), and the population difference (C145-C146) is a valid consideration. However, this finding contradicts established evidence (C57) and may reflect study limitations rather than true lack of efficacy.

results.result: Pancreatic stent placement was classified as a 'procedure on the pancreatic duct' rather than as prophylaxis because it is itself a higher-risk procedure for PEP than biliary procedures without pancreatic duct access, and it was performed alongside other high-risk procedures (guidewire placement or pancreatography).
results.evaluation: Claims C91-C92 and C147-C148 explain the classification decision with supporting data (Supplementary file 2) and citations. This approach is methodologically sound given that pancreatic stent placement requires pancreatic duct access and is used as prophylaxis after such access has already occurred.

results.result: The SuPER model is a simple 5-item preprocedural risk score that can predict PEP risk before ERCP and may aid in clinical decision-making by enabling selection of appropriate expert endoscopists and prophylactic measures for high-risk patients.
results.evaluation: Claims C67-C70, C102-C103, C138, and C153-C154 describe the model's characteristics and potential clinical utility. The simplicity (5 items, easily assessed) and preprocedural applicability are supported by the study design and results. The clinical utility statements (C68-C70, C154) are appropriately qualified as potential benefits ('may aid').

results.result: The study has limitations including its retrospective design with missing data, though the percentage of excluded patients (<5%) and missing data (<1%) were minimal. Patients with missing data for selected variables were removed from analysis. The retrospective design prevented collection of detailed cannulation data.
results.evaluation: Claims C77-C78 and C64-C65, C82, C118-C119 appropriately acknowledge study limitations. The low rates of exclusion and missing data (C64-C65) support data quality, and the handling of missing data (C82) is appropriate. The inability to assess cannulation attempts (C118-C119) is a recognized limitation of retrospective studies.

results.result: The study was conducted only in Japan using multicenter data, and the authors acknowledge that prospective validation studies over wider geographical regions are needed in the future.
results.evaluation: Claims C79-C81 appropriately identify geographic limitation and need for external validation. This is a standard limitation for prediction models that requires acknowledgment and future work.

results.result: The model can predict PEP risk regardless of whether pancreatic duct procedures are performed, because additional procedures can be conducted during ERCP and unplanned pancreatography often occurs. The score can be calculated with or without planned pancreatic duct procedures.
results.evaluation: Claims C150-C152 describe an important feature of the model - its flexibility in handling planned vs. unplanned pancreatic duct procedures. This is supported by the model design (C14) which treats this as 'planned pancreatic duct procedures' for pre-ERCP calculation, and Figure 2 which shows how to calculate both scenarios.

results.result: Statistical methods included Cochran-Armitage trend test for correlation analysis, C-statistic for discrimination, Hosmer-Lemeshow test for calibration, and multivariate logistic regression for independence assessment. Analyses were performed using EZR version 1.62 and SPSS version 26.0, with p<0.05 considered significant.
results.evaluation: Claims C126-C131 describe appropriate statistical methods for prediction model development and validation. The methods are standard for this type of analysis, software versions are specified, and the significance threshold is clearly stated.

results.result: PEP is a severe and potentially deadly complication of ERCP, with occurrence rates of 3.1-13.0% and fatality rates of 0.1-0.7%. ERCP-related procedures are relatively risky among endoscopic procedures, with major adverse events including perforation, bleeding, and PEP.
results.evaluation: Claims C1-C3 and C72-C74 provide well-established background information about PEP severity and ERCP risks, supported by multiple citations to prior literature. These claims establish the clinical importance of the research question.

results.result: Six previous PEP risk scoring systems have been developed since 2002, but the ideal method for predicting PEP risk before ERCP has not yet been identified. The first system (2002) identified pain during procedure, pancreatic duct cannulation, history of PEP, and number of cannulation attempts as risk factors.
results.evaluation: Claims C4-C6 and C104 provide appropriate context from prior literature with supporting citations. The statement that no ideal preprocedural method exists (C104) justifies the current study's objective.

results.result: One previous scoring system included sphincter of Oddi dysfunction (SOD) as a test item, which requires sphincter of Oddi manometry (not widely used) and fulfillment of criteria for biliary pain (8 items) and SOD (15 items), making it complex and impractical.
results.evaluation: Claims C139-C143 provide valid criticism of a prior scoring system's complexity, supported by citation (DiMagno et al., 2013; Cotton et al., 2016). This comparison highlights the advantage of the SuPER model's simplicity.

results.result: The study was approved by institutional review boards (Fukushima Medical University and partner institutions, number 2453). Anonymous clinical data were used after patients provided written consent for treatment, so additional informed consent for the study was not required. Study details are available on the Fukushima Medical University homepage.
results.evaluation: Claims C22 and C106-C108 describe appropriate ethical procedures for a retrospective study using anonymized data. The waiver of additional consent is reasonable given the retrospective design and data anonymization.

results.result: The study is a multicenter retrospective study conducted at six institutions in Japan, enrolling 2074 patients who underwent ERCP between November 2020 and October 2022, with 1037 patients randomly assigned to each of the development and validation cohorts. The study excluded 102 patients for various reasons including history of choledochojejunostomy, acute pancreatitis, and other conditions.
results.evaluation: Both reviewers acknowledge this is a 'solid retrospective' study but emphasize significant limitations. The editor notes it is 'a solid retrospective single-center study in one country' requiring future validation 'in many countries and on large numbers of patients.' The anonymous reviewer similarly states it is 'a single-country, retrospective study' and notes 'many cases were excluded, so the score cannot be applied to those patients,' indicating concerns about generalizability and applicability.

results.result: The SuPER model consists of five pre-procedural risk factors that can be identified before ERCP: pancreatic calcification (-2 points), female sex (1 point), intraductal papillary mucinous neoplasm (2 points), native papilla of Vater (2 points), and pancreatic duct procedures (2 points). These factors were identified through multivariate logistic regression analysis in the development cohort and can be easily assessed via medical interviews and imaging.
results.evaluation: Both reviewers explicitly recognize the model's value as a pre-procedural prediction tool. The editor describes it as 'a new score for predicting post-ERCP pancreatitis' that 'offers an idea about the risk of pancreatitis before the procedure,' distinguishing it from 'most scores [that] depend on intraprocedural maneuvers.' The anonymous reviewer emphasizes this as a key strength, stating it 'provides a new general tool for predicting post-ERCP pancreatitis before the procedure' and notes the model 'can help with the maneuver' by identifying high-risk patients.

results.result: In the development cohort, the SuPER model stratified patients into three risk groups with PEP occurrence rates of 0% for low-risk patients (≤0 points, 0/327), 5.5% for moderate-risk patients (1-3 points, 27/492), and 20.2% for high-risk patients (4-7 points, 39/193). The model showed good discrimination with a C statistic of 0.77 (95% CI 0.72-0.82) and good calibration (Hosmer-Lemeshow test p=0.59).
results.evaluation: Reviewers accept the risk stratification findings without critique. The anonymous reviewer explicitly notes as a strength that 'this paper provides a model for stratifying patients before the ERCP procedure into low, moderate, and high risk for pancreatitis' and that 'depending on this score that identifies low, moderate, and high-risk patients for post-pancreatitis, so from the start, experienced and well-trained endoscopists can do the procedure.' The editor similarly acknowledges the model's ability to stratify risk before the procedure.

results.result: In the validation cohort, the SuPER model maintained acceptable performance with a C statistic of 0.71 (95% CI 0.64-0.78) and good calibration (Hosmer-Lemeshow test p=0.40). PEP rates in the validation cohort were 2.4% (8/331) for low-risk, 5.3% (27/513) for moderate-risk, and 18.0% (29/161) for high-risk patients, with significant correlation between risk classification and PEP occurrence (p<0.01).
results.evaluation: While reviewers do not directly challenge the validation results, both emphasize the need for broader validation. The editor states 'to be validated in the future, this score will need to be done in many countries and on large numbers of patients.' The anonymous reviewer similarly notes 'to be validated, this score should be done in many countries and on large numbers of patients,' suggesting the current single-country validation is insufficient for establishing generalizability.

results.result: The PEP risk classification was a significant independent predictive factor for PEP (OR 4.2, 95% CI 2.8-6.3; p<0.01) even after adjusting for intraprocedural risk factors (precut sphincterotomy and inadvertent pancreatic duct cannulation), which themselves were not significantly associated with PEP occurrence in this study.
results.evaluation: Reviewers implicitly accept this finding by emphasizing the model's pre-procedural nature as a key advantage. The editor notes 'most scores depend on intraprocedural maneuvers, such as the number of attempts to cannulate the papilla,' positioning this model's independence from intraprocedural factors as a strength. The anonymous reviewer similarly emphasizes 'most scores depend on the intraprocedural maneuver' while this study 'discusses a new preprocedural score,' indicating acceptance of the model's independence from procedural factors.

results.result: The SuPER model may aid in predicting and explaining PEP risk before ERCP, allowing selection of appropriate expert endoscopists, useful prophylaxes, and alternative procedures for high-risk patients, thereby potentially preventing PEP.
results.evaluation: Reviewers explicitly endorse the clinical utility claims. The anonymous reviewer states as a strength that 'depending on this score that identifies low, moderate, and high-risk patients for post-pancreatitis, so from the start, experienced and well-trained endoscopists can do the procedure or can refer patients to tertiary hospitals or use interventional radiology.' The editor similarly acknowledges the model helps identify when 'experienced endoscopists can do the procedure from the start,' supporting the proposed clinical applications.

results.result: In the development cohort, 70 patients (6.8%) were diagnosed with PEP (60 mild, 8 moderate, 2 severe), and in the validation cohort, 64 patients (6.2%) were diagnosed with PEP, with most cases being mild severity.
results.evaluation: Reviewers do not question the PEP incidence or severity distribution. The anonymous reviewer notes 'the number of patients in this study is sufficient to analyze data correctly' as a strength, implicitly accepting the observed PEP rates and their distribution across severity categories.

results.result: PEP diagnosis and severity were assessed according to Cotton's criteria, with patients diagnosed if they experienced abdominal pain and hyperamylasemia (>3× normal upper limit) at least 24 hours after ERCP, and severity classified as mild (2-3 days hospitalization extension), moderate (4-10 days), or severe (>10 days or complications).
results.evaluation: Reviewers do not challenge the diagnostic criteria or severity classification. The use of standard Cotton's criteria is implicitly accepted as appropriate methodology, with no concerns raised about outcome definition.

results.result: The ideal method for predicting PEP risk before ERCP has yet to be identified, and prospective validation studies over wider geographical regions are needed in the future.
results.evaluation: Both reviewers explicitly agree with this limitation and future direction. The editor states 'to be validated in the future, this score will need to be done in many countries and on large numbers of patients.' The anonymous reviewer similarly emphasizes 'to be validated, this score should be done in many countries and on large numbers of patients,' and in comments on the revised version notes concern about 'depending on old references' and suggests testing 'the validity of that score against, if present, a proven score to check its validity.'

results.result: The percentage of patients who did not meet inclusion criteria was not greater than 5%, the percentage of missing data was not greater than 1%, and patients with missing data for variables selected in the risk score model were removed from the final cohort.
results.evaluation: While the authors claim minimal missing data, the anonymous reviewer raises concern that 'many cases were excluded, so the score cannot be applied to those patients,' suggesting the exclusions may limit applicability. The reviewer does not directly challenge the data quality claims but questions the practical implications of the exclusion criteria.

results.result: Six previous scoring systems for predicting PEP risk have been devised since 2002, with the first system identifying pain during procedure, pancreatic duct cannulation, history of PEP, and number of cannulation attempts as risk factors. One previous system included sphincter of Oddi dysfunction (SOD) as a test item, which requires complex diagnostic criteria (8 items for biliary pain, 15 items for SOD) and sphincter of Oddi manometry that is not widely used.
results.evaluation: The anonymous reviewer questions the adequacy of the literature review in comments on the revised version, stating 'depending on old references cannot help us know the current situation. What if there are better more recent predictive tools? It would be better to test the validity of that score against, if present, a proven score to check its validity.' This suggests concern that the comparison to existing scoring systems may be incomplete or outdated.
